title: Tracing the dynamics of misinformation and vaccine stance in Finland amid COVID-19
screen_reason: Computational content analysis of 1,683,700 Finnish-language vaccine-related tweets (1 December 2019 - 24 October 2022). A FinBERT classifier, fine-tuned on 4,150 human-annotated tweets, labelled 460,087 tweets as misinformation, 'over 27% of the dataset'. Share of items in a sample classified as false or conspiratorial, with a stated denominator, so CONTENT. A second, human-coded share is available on the annotation subsample (709/4,150).

estimates.measure_type: % of Finnish-language vaccine-related tweets classified as containing misinformation by a fine-tuned FinBERT classifier
estimates.value_raw: 460,087 of 1,683,700 tweets, stated as 'over 27% of the dataset' (460,087/1,683,700 = 27.3%)
estimates.denominator: 1,683,700 Finnish vaccine/COVID-related tweets from 60,560 unique accounts (724,214 retweets, 57,865 quoted, 901,621 original), retrieved with 147 query keywords built from 14 Finnish seed terms
estimates.definition: A tweet was labelled 1 when the classifier's softmax probability exceeded the tuned threshold for the binary category 'the content of the tweet contained or related to misinformation'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "In this study, misinformation is defined as any false, inaccurate, or conspiratorial information pertaining to COVID-19 and vaccination."
estimates.source_quote: The sentiment classification model indicates 446,400 tweets with NSV, which is almost 27% of our dataset. Similarly, the misinformation classification model identifies 460,087 tweets as misinformation, accounting for over 27% of the dataset.
estimates.page_loc: Methods, 'Text classification' (p. 198); also the abstract and Discussion
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four native Finnish research assistants manually labelled 4,150 tweets drawn at random from the corpus (Finnish, not a retweet, over 30 characters), trained over six iterative sessions; average Krippendorff's alpha 0.668 for misinformation and 0.693 for stance, which the authors class as good. Annotation followed the COVID-19 misinformation codebook of Memon and Carley (2020) plus fact-checking sites and the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare webpage. A FinBERT model fine-tuned on these labels (weighted loss, tuned threshold) was applied to the whole corpus; the misinformation classifier reached accuracy 0.85 and F1 0.67 on the test set, against 0.94 and 0.89 for the stance classifier.
estimates.moderator_quote: For the data collection, we constructed 147 query keywords from a set of 14 Finnish terms through conjugation, inflection, and phrasing. Utilizing the R package academictwitteR (Barrie & Ho, 2021), we extracted tweets containing any of the query keywords between 1st December 2019 and 24th October 2022. These search categories generated a total of 1,683,700 tweets from 60,560 unique Twitter accounts.
estimates.notes: 27.3% is computed from the two verbatim counts with the same denominator, which R8 permits; the paper states only 'over 27%'. Confidence is medium because the misinformation classifier's F1 is 0.67 (accuracy 0.85), so the labelled share carries substantial classification error, and the corpus includes retweets while the human training set excluded them. The abstract and Discussion round this to 'approximately a third' and 'roughly one in three tweets', which overstates the 27.3% the reported counts give; the counts are used here. year 2021 is the midpoint of the December 2019 - October 2022 collection window, chosen as the representative point for a whole-period estimate; the paper also shows the ratio rising over time (Figure 2).

estimates.date: 1 December 2019 - 24 October 2022 (annotation subsample drawn from the same window)
estimates.measure_type: % of randomly drawn Finnish original tweets hand-labelled by native-speaker annotators as containing misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 709 of 4,150 tweets (the paper prints this as '709 (0.17%)', a proportion misformatted as a percentage; 709/4,150 = 17.1%)
estimates.denominator: 4,150 tweets chosen at random from the same corpus subject to three inclusion criteria: written in Finnish, not a retweet, and longer than 30 characters
estimates.definition: Human annotators assigned the tweet to the category 'the content of the tweet contained or related to misinformation', following the Memon and Carley (2020) COVID-19 misinformation codebook.
estimates.misinfo_def: "In this study, misinformation is defined as any false, inaccurate, or conspiratorial information pertaining to COVID-19 and vaccination."
estimates.source_quote: From 4150 tweets, the manual annotation labels 1118 (0.27%) tweets with NSV and 709 (0.17%) tweets
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four native Finnish research assistants, trained over six iterative sessions, with inter-rater reliability assessed each session; average Krippendorff's alpha 0.668 for misinformation (the authors' own scale calls 0.67-0.8 good and below 0.5 poor, so this sits at the boundary). Annotation used the Memon and Carley (2020) COVID-19 misinformation codebook, supplemented by fact-checking sites and the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare webpage.
estimates.moderator_quote: In the initial stage of assembling the training data, four native Finnish research assistants manually labeled 4150 texts for both categories. The training data were randomly chosen from the primary dataset, adhering to the following inclusion criteria: the tweet must be written in Finnish, not be a retweet, and exceed 30 characters in length.
estimates.notes: The sentence ends 'containing misinformation'; the text file breaks that word with a soft hyphen, so the quoted span stops just before it. Kept as a separate row because it is the same construct measured with a different ground truth on a different denominator: human coders on a random subsample of original Finnish tweets (17.1%) versus the classifier on the whole corpus including retweets (27.3%). The ten-point gap is worth an adjudicator's attention; it may reflect the retweet exclusion, the length filter, or classifier error (F1 0.67). Not marked definition_variant because the misinformation definition is identical, only the instrument and the eligible tweets differ. Risk to note: this subsample was assembled as classifier training data, and although the paper says it was randomly chosen, training sets are sometimes enriched, which would inflate the share.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Negative Stance towards Vaccines (446,400 tweets, 'almost 27%'; 1,118/4,150 = 26.9% in the human subsample) is a stance measure, not falsity, so no row. (2) Bot prevalence (13,522 bot accounts = 22.3% of 60,560 accounts; 4,894 malicious bots = 8% of accounts) counts automation, not misinformation exposure or sharing; the malicious-bot definition is 'bot accounts explicitly established for disseminating misinformation or expressing NSV', which mixes falsity with stance, so it is not a clean SHARING actor_share either. (3) A CONCENTRATION row was considered and rejected: the paper says malicious bots 'played a rising role, albeit less than 1%' and that 'a minority of accounts disseminated a vast quantity' of misinformation, but 'less than 1%' is a bound rather than a point, its referent (share of all COVID tweets vs share of misinformation tweets) is not pinned down in the text, and pairing it with the 8% account figure would be my inference. R1 requires a stated group share and a stated activity share. (4) Figure 2's 'over 30% of tweets at the end of 2022 containing some form of NSV or misinformation' is a combined stance-or-misinformation measure read off a line chart at one time point; not extracted. (5) Time-series values for the misinformation ratio are only visible in Figures 2 and 3 without data labels; the whole-period figure is used instead, as the instructions direct for time series. (6) The abstract's 'approximately a third' and the Discussion's 'roughly one in three' are inconsistent with the reported counts (27.3%) and were not used.

rob.design: Longitudinal computational content analysis of Twitter. Frame: all tweets matching any of 147 Finnish query keywords built from 14 seed terms (korona, rokote, mrna, Pfizer, Biontech, Moderna, piikki, AstraZeneca, kuole, injektio, rokotushaitta, myrkkypiikki, covid, toinen rokotus), 1 December 2019 - 24 October 2022, collected with academictwitteR: 1,683,700 tweets from 60,560 accounts. Labelling: 4,150 randomly drawn tweets hand-annotated by four native Finnish assistants over six training rounds (Krippendorff's alpha 0.668 misinformation, 0.693 stance), used to fine-tune FinBERT (chosen over logistic regression and LSTM); misinformation classifier accuracy 0.85, F1 0.67; stance classifier accuracy 0.94, F1 0.89. Bot detection with Botometer v4 (CAP >= 0.804), validated on 100 manually annotated accounts at 0.87 accuracy, with the authors noting known Botometer mislabelling of government, newspaper and politician accounts. Authors' stated limitations: Twitter is not representative of the general population, the design is correlational, and the Finnish focus limits generalisability. No weighting toward exposure or audience, so the estimate is a share of posted items, not of what anyone saw.
rob.item6_quote: In this study, misinformation is defined as any false, inaccurate, or conspiratorial information pertaining to COVID-19 and vaccination. Our research was not designed to make distinctions between misinformation and disinformation or between various types of misinformation, including sarcasm, fraudulent treatments/cures, panic buying, and conspiracy theories.
rob.item10_quote: Similarly, the misinformation classification model identifies 460,087 tweets as misinformation, accounting for over 27% of the dataset.
